content: Biosalinity refers to the scientific study and practical application of using saline (salty) water for the irrigation of agricultural crops. In many arid and semi-arid regions, water sources are available, but the water is often brackish, containing 500 to 5000 parts per million (ppm) of salt by weight, or saline, with a salt concentration of 3-5%. These water sources may exist in underground aquifers or as seawater along coastal deserts. Traditional farming methods are not well-suited for saline water use, as it leads to soil salinization, which makes the soil unsuitable for cultivating most crop plants. Historically, arid and semi-arid regions were deemed unsuitable for agriculture, and systematic agricultural development in these areas was not pursued until the latter half of the 20th century. Research in the field of biosalinity encompasses several areas. These include investigations into the biochemical and physiological mechanisms that enable plants to tolerate salt, as well as breeding and selecting plants for enhanced salt tolerance, a trait known as halotolerance. Scientists also study specific periods in a crop plant's life cycle when it may exhibit reduced sensitivity to salt. Additionally, saline irrigation water can be used strategically to enhance desirable traits in crops, such as increasing sugar concentration in fruits or controlling the ripening process. Other areas of research include examining the interactions between salinity and soil properties and developing naturally salt-tolerant plant species, known as halophytes, into viable agricultural crops. Halophilic bacteria, which thrive in high-salinity environments, are also of interest in this context. When saline or brackish water irrigation is applied correctly—such as by irrigating in amounts that exceed the rate of evapotranspiration and maintaining soil structure to ensure proper drainage—it does not necessarily lead to increased soil salinization. In some cases, farmers may need to apply additional water after a rainstorm to flush salts below the root zone, thereby preventing salt accumulation in the soil.
